articles.title: New study reveals that fluctuating—not just intense—brain signals play a hidden role in overeating
articles.summary: A recent study links inconsistent brain reward signals to higher body weight and erratic eating patterns. The research suggests that fluctuating neural responses, rather than consistently strong cravings, may drive overeating and certain eating disorders.

articles.title: Humor makes taboo words less distracting
articles.summary: Taboo words usually derail our focus, slowing down cognitive tasks. However, new research reveals a surprising twist: when profanity is funny, it becomes significantly less distracting, highlighting a fascinating link between humor, arousal, and attention.

articles.title: Sexual objectification does not erase the perceived humanity of OnlyFans creators, study suggests
articles.summary: People who sell explicit digital content online are heavily sexually objectified by observers, yet they are still viewed as capable individuals with free will. These findings challenge traditional psychological assumptions about objectification and dehumanization.

articles.title: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases
articles.summary: A large study tracking more than 95,000 people suggests that how you sleep may be linked to your risk of developing dozens of diseases. People who spent more time in REM sleep had lower risks of 83 conditions, including dementia, heart failure, and Parkinson’s disease, while more deep sleep was associated with lower risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes and major depression.

articles.title: Rare pregnancy infections may triple the risk of autism
articles.summary: A major Swedish study of 3.7 million people has found that rare TORCH infections passed from a pregnant woman to the fetus are linked to much higher risks of autism and intellectual disability later in life. Children with a congenital TORCH infection were about three times more likely to be diagnosed with autism, more than seven times more likely to have an intellectual disability, and up to 30 times more likely to have severe to profound intellectual disability.

articles.title: Parents’ genetic traits might indirectly influence a child’s risk for anxiety and depression
articles.summary: A child's risk of developing anxiety and depression is influenced by both the genes they inherit and the genetic traits of their parents, revealing how a parent's DNA shapes the environment they create for their children.

articles.title: Personal hardship and online isolation predict support for white nationalism
articles.summary: Over 13 percent of young white men in the U.S. endorse the core ideas of white nationalism. New research suggests this support is fueled by economic strain and internet isolation, not neighborhood diversity.

articles.title: A specific narcissistic trait predicts aggression in socially anxious individuals
articles.summary: While social anxiety is often associated with quiet avoidance, a new study reveals that highly socially anxious people with self-centered traits are more likely to react to social threats with both impulsive and calculated aggression.

articles.title: When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable
articles.summary: The brain may have a built-in way to quickly settle disagreements between regions processing the same scene. Researchers found that matching signals between two visual areas lasted longer, while conflicting signals rapidly faded away. This “consensus building” mechanism could help explain how the brain turns many specialized inputs into one unified view of the world.

articles.title: First fMRI study of mescaline reveals altered sensory filtering and brain networks
articles.summary: A groundbreaking brain imaging study in awake rats reveals that the psychedelic mescaline uniquely alters brain function. The drug reduces cerebellum activity while boosting global connectivity, shifting how the brain processes rewards and filters sensory information.

articles.title: Fear of the unknown is linked to lower life satisfaction and heightened death anxiety
articles.summary: People who struggle with uncertainty tend to report lower life satisfaction. According to new research, this link is deeply existential, intertwining a fear of the unknown with a lower sense of purpose and higher death anxiety.
